simulations.title: First Day at a Welding Workshop
simulations.scenario: Meet the workshop team and complete onboarding safely.

mission.title: First Day at the Workshop
mission.welcome: Welcome to the team. Today is your first day. You will meet your supervisor, learn workshop safety, introduce yourself, and complete your onboarding.
mission.shadowRecommendation: Open Shadow and practise the workplace lines for this stage — hear each one, then say it back.

nextMission.title: Shift Handover
nextMission.preview: Tomorrow you'll explain completed work, report issues, and communicate with the next welding team.

unexpectedEvents.message: Sorry to jump in — Daniel, we've got a rush job landed. You're the new one, yeah? Can you give me a hand once you're set up?

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat this onboarding simulation and strengthen one missed objective.

openings.hr: Good morning — you must be the new welder. I'm Maya from HR. Tell me a little about yourself and the work you've done.
openings.supervisor: Morning. Daniel, I run this shop. Before I put you on anything, tell me what you've been welding.
openings.coworker: Hey — you're the new one, right? I'm Luis. What kind of work were you doing before this?
openings.safety: Morning. Priya, safety officer. Everyone gets five minutes with me on day one. Tell me about your experience first.
openings.qa: You're new — I'm Amelia, I inspect what leaves this shop. Tell me where you've worked and what you welded.

turns.text: Good. We run a lot of structural work here. What positions are you comfortable in?
Before you touch a machine — walk me through what you check to work safely.
One more thing. If you're not sure about a job, who do you go to? We'd rather you ask.
I check every weld that leaves here. If I send something back, how would you want me to tell you?

closing.text: That's everything from us. Welcome to the team — go and find Daniel, he'll get you started.

open.ask: Tell me about yourself and the work you've done.

points.label: Say who you are and that you are a welder
Say how long you have been doing it
Name the processes you actually run
Say what you welded — product or sector
End with what you are looking for or ready to do

open.model: I'm a welder with six years' experience. I mostly run MIG and stick on structural steel — beams, columns and brackets for building frames. The last two years I was on a fabrication shop floor doing fit-up and welding, and I'm looking for work where I can move onto pipe.
open.why: This is the answer every employer hears first, and most welders lose the job here by being too short. Four facts in twenty seconds: who you are, how long, which processes, what you welded.
open.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t0.ask: We run a lot of structural work here. What positions are you comfortable in?

points.label: Name the positions you can weld
Be honest about what you are still weak in
Say you are willing to be tested or to learn

t0.model: I'm comfortable flat and horizontal, and vertical up on fillet welds. Overhead I can do but I'm slower, so I'd want some practice before you put me on it. I'm happy to do a test piece so you can see for yourself.
t0.why: Never claim a position you cannot hold — you will be found out on the test piece. Saying what you cannot do yet, and offering to be tested, reads as professional, not weak.
t0.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t1.ask: Before you touch a machine — walk me through what you check to work safely.

points.label: Say what you check around you
Say you check the equipment and leads
Say you ask if something is unclear

t1.model: First my PPE — helmet, gloves, sleeves and boots. Then the area: nothing flammable near, screens up so I don't flash anyone, and extraction on for fume. Then the set itself — leads and earth clamp in good order, no damaged insulation. If anything doesn't look right I stop and ask the supervisor.
t1.why: Safety answers are judged on order and specifics: yourself, the area, the equipment, then who you tell. Vague answers like 'I always work safely' score nothing anywhere in the world.
t1.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t2.ask: If you're not sure about a job, who do you go to? We'd rather you ask.

points.label: Name a role you would go to
Say you stop rather than guess
Say why asking is better than guessing

t2.model: I go to the supervisor, or the inspector if it's a quality question. I'd rather stop and ask for two minutes than guess and have the whole piece cut out later. Asking is cheaper than rework.
t2.why: Employers abroad are testing one thing here: will this person guess silently? Say the role, say you stop first, and give the reason.
t2.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t3.ask: I check every weld that leaves here. If I send something back, how would you want me to tell you?

points.label: Ask for the specific defect and location
Say what you would do next
Say you want to avoid repeating it

t3.model: Tell me straight, I'd rather know. Show me where it is and what's wrong with it — undercut, porosity, whatever it is — and I'll grind it out and re-run it. And tell me why it happened so I don't put the same fault in the next one.
t3.why: How a welder takes rejection is watched closely on every site. Accept it, ask for specifics, state the fix, ask what caused it.
t3.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

regulatory.requirement: Mandatory workshop safety orientation, hazard communication, emergency exit verification, and allocation of flame-resistant PPE.

benchmarks.must: Identify the emergency assembly point, eye-wash station and fire extinguishers
Name the minimum PPE: auto-darkening helmet with correct shade rating, leather gloves, flame-resistant jacket, steel-toe boots
Review the workshop-specific safety rules before turning on any machinery

simulations.title: Shift Handover
simulations.scenario: Give your team a useful handover before the next shift.

unexpectedEvents.message: Hang on. Night shift just rang, they're two hands down. Does that change what you'd hand over?

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Shift Handover and make your update more concise.

openings.supervisor: Before you go — give me the handover. What did you finish today?
openings.coworker: I'm taking over from you. What's left on the job?
openings.qa: I'm logging tonight's handover. Tell me what's complete and what's still open.
openings.safety: Handover time. Anything on your shift I need to know about?
openings.hr: I'm sitting in on handovers this week. Talk me through your day as if I were the next shift.

turns.text: Got it. Anything that gave you trouble? I'd rather hear it now than find it at ten o'clock.
Which joints have I still got to inspect?
And what do you want the night shift to start with?
Anything left in the area that could catch someone out?

closing.text: Clear handover. That's what I want every night. Go home.

open.ask: Before you go — give me the handover. What did you finish today?

points.label: Say which job, joint or drawing number

open.model: I finished the six fillet joints on spool twelve and they're ready for inspection. Spool thirteen is fitted and tacked but not welded. One thing to know — we ran short of three-point-two rods this afternoon, so that's why thirteen stopped.
open.why: A handover is judged on whether the next person can start work without ringing you. Finished, where, what's left, what went wrong.
open.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t0.ask: Anything that gave you trouble? I'd rather hear it now than find it at ten o'clock.

points.label: Say what state you left it in

t0.model: The wire feed on set four kept slipping, so I lost about an hour. I've tagged it and written it in the log so nobody picks it up cold in the morning.
t0.why: Reporting trouble late is how small faults become expensive ones. Name it, say the effect, say what state you left it in.
t0.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t1.ask: Which joints have I still got to inspect?

points.label: Say which are not ready yet

t1.model: Joints one to six on spool twelve are ready — cleaned and marked up. Seven and eight are welded but I haven't cleaned them yet, so leave those until the morning.
t1.why: Inspectors work from a weld map. Speaking in joint numbers rather than 'that one over there' is what makes you easy to work with.
t1.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t2.ask: And what do you want the night shift to start with?
t2.model: Start them on spool thirteen — it's already fitted and tacked, so they can go straight to welding. Tell them to check the fit-up on the last joint first, I wasn't happy with the gap.
t2.why: One priority, one reason, one warning. Giving three equal tasks means the night shift picks the easiest.
t2.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t3.ask: Anything left in the area that could catch someone out?

points.label: Say what you did about it

t3.model: The plate on the bench is still hot — I've put a hot-work sign on it. Otherwise leads are coiled and the bottles are closed off and chained.
t3.why: A safety handover is not a formality: name the hazard, what you did, and what is still live.
t3.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

codes.title: Quality requirements for fusion welding of metallic materials

regulatory.requirement: Continuous workflow traceability. Incoming shifts must be briefed on active weld setups, machine state, material trace numbers and production anomalies.

benchmarks.must: State the equipment status: duty cycle limits, machine settings or gas cylinder pressures
Identify the joint or job ID on the bench and its phase of completion
Report anomalies, defect trends, or instructions left by the outgoing supervisor

simulations.title: Equipment Readiness Check
simulations.scenario: Prepare equipment and report an issue before work starts.

unexpectedEvents.message: Don't touch that grinder — I've just seen the guard's cracked.

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Equipment Readiness Check and sharpen your issue report.

openings.supervisor: That machine's yours for the day. Tell me how you'd check it over before you start.
openings.coworker: That set's been playing up. What do you look at first?
openings.safety: Before you power anything up — talk me through your checks.
openings.qa: Your settings matter for what I inspect later. What are you setting up, and why?
openings.hr: You mentioned equipment in your interview. Talk me through how you get set up for a shift.

turns.text: Say the wire feed keeps slipping. How would you report that?
If a machine isn't right, what do you do — carry on, or stop?
And how would you make sure nobody else uses it in the meantime?
Tell me what you'd write in the log.

closing.text: Good. You check it, you flag it, you don't guess. That's how we run.

open.ask: That machine's yours for the day. Tell me how you'd check it over before you start.

points.label: Check the settings against the job

open.model: I look at the leads first — any cuts in the insulation and it doesn't get used. Then the earth clamp, that it's on clean metal and tight. Then gas flow and the contact tip. Last I set the amps and volts for the job and run a test piece if I can.
open.why: Equipment checks are a sequence, and saying them in order shows you actually do them. Power, earth, consumables, settings.
open.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t0.ask: Say the wire feed keeps slipping. How would you report that?

points.label: Say exactly what the machine is doing
Say what you do in the meantime

t0.model: I'd say the wire is slipping at the drive rolls, mostly after a long run, and it's putting birdnests in the liner. I'd report it to the supervisor and maintenance, tag the set so nobody else picks it up, and move to another machine until it's looked at.
t0.why: A fault report that says only 'it's not working' gets ignored. What, when, who you told, what you did meanwhile.
t0.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t1.ask: If a machine isn't right, what do you do — carry on, or stop?
t1.model: I stop. A set that isn't running right either hurts somebody or puts a defect in the weld, and both cost more than an hour's downtime. I tag it and tell the supervisor.
t1.why: There is only one right answer here and every employer is listening for it. Say 'I stop' first, then justify it.
t1.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t2.ask: And how would you make sure nobody else uses it in the meantime?

points.label: Say you tag, label or lock it
Say you isolate the power or gas

t2.model: Tag on the machine, power isolated, and I tell the shift and write it on the board. A tag on its own isn't enough if the next man doesn't read it.
t2.why: Isolation is physical plus communication. Saying both is what separates a trained welder from someone repeating a phrase.
t2.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t3.ask: Tell me what you'd write in the log.
t3.model: Set four, bay two. Wire feed slipping intermittently from about two o'clock. Machine tagged and isolated, supervisor and maintenance informed. Signed and dated.
t3.why: A log entry is a record someone may read months later. Machine, fault, time, action, name.
t3.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

codes.title: Fabrication requirements
codes.note: Clause numbering follows AWS D1.1 editions before 2020; the 2020 edition renumbered Fabrication to Clause 7 and Inspection to Clause 8. Confirm against the edition in force on your project.

regulatory.requirement: Inspection of insulation, cable damage, gas delivery systems and ground clamp connections before striking an arc, to prevent shock hazards and porous welds.

benchmarks.must: Confirm welding cables are free of exposed copper, deep cuts or faulty splices
Check the gas delivery system for leaks and that cylinders are chained securely upright
Validate ground clamp placement for a stable electrical loop and clean current transmission

simulations.title: Material Preparation Briefing
simulations.scenario: Clarify materials and preparation before a job.

unexpectedEvents.message: Stop there a second. The label on that plate doesn't match the drawing.

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Material Preparation Briefing and improve specification language.

openings.supervisor: Materials are on the bench. Tell me how you'd get them ready.
openings.coworker: We're prepping together today. What do you want to start on?
openings.qa: Preparation is where most of my rejects come from. Talk me through yours.
openings.safety: Before you cut or grind anything, tell me what you'd sort out first.
openings.hr: Describe a job where preparation made the difference. I want to hear how you explain it.

turns.text: How would you tell me the fit-up isn't right?
If the material isn't what the job called for, who do you tell?
And if I've prepped it differently to you — how do we sort that out?
Anything about this prep that could put someone at risk?

closing.text: That's the standard. Get the prep right and the rest follows.

open.ask: Materials are on the bench. Tell me how you'd get them ready.

points.label: Check the material is the right one
Say how you prepare the edge or fit
Say you check it against the drawing

open.model: First I check the plate is the grade the job calls for — the marking against the drawing. Then clean the prep back to bright metal, no scale, rust or paint. Then set the bevel and the root gap to the procedure and tack it up, checking alignment before I run anything.
open.why: Most rejected welds are made before the arc is struck. Identify, clean, prepare, check against the drawing.
open.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t0.ask: How would you tell me the fit-up isn't right?

points.label: Say what is wrong with it

t0.model: The root gap's opened up to about five mil at the top end — the drawing says three. There's a bit of hi-lo with it too. Do you want it re-tacked, or shall I build the root up?
t0.why: Reporting a problem without a measurement forces the supervisor to come and look. Say what, how much, where, then ask for the decision.
t0.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t1.ask: If the material isn't what the job called for, who do you tell?

points.label: Say you do not weld it

t1.model: I stop and don't weld it. I'd take it to the supervisor and the inspector, because if the grade is wrong the procedure doesn't apply and the joint could fail. Substituting material isn't my call.
t1.why: Material substitution is one of the fastest ways to lose a job internationally. Stop, escalate, and say plainly that it is not your decision.
t1.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t2.ask: And if I've prepped it differently to you — how do we sort that out?

points.label: Go back to the drawing or procedure
Say you talk it through rather than argue
Say who decides if you disagree

t2.model: We both go back to the drawing and the procedure — whatever it says wins, not whichever of us is louder. If it's genuinely unclear we take it to the supervisor rather than each doing our own thing.
t2.why: Disagreement between welders is normal. The answer employers want is that the document decides, not seniority.
t2.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t3.ask: Anything about this prep that could put someone at risk?

points.label: Name a real hazard from prep work
Say how you protect yourself and others

t3.model: Grinding throws sparks and dust, so goggles and a mask for me, and screens up so I'm not throwing sparks at whoever's behind me. If there's galvanising on it that's a fume problem and it needs extraction.
t3.why: Naming the hazard from the specific task, and then the people around you, is what a safety officer is listening for.
t3.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

codes.title: Inspection documents for metallic products (mill certificates)

regulatory.requirement: Alignment of joint geometry, base metal cleanliness and mill test report traceability before assembly.

benchmarks.must: Verify the base metal type against the Material Test Report or mill certificate
Remove surface contaminants — rust, oil, scale, moisture — with a dedicated wire brush or grinder to prevent porosity
Cross-check the bevel angle, root opening and root face against the job specification

simulations.title: Safety Stop-Work Conversation
simulations.scenario: Identify a hazard and use calm stop-work communication.

unexpectedEvents.message: Extraction's just cut out. Whole line, not only your bay.

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Safety Stop-Work Conversation and make the action more direct.

openings.safety: You flagged something on line two. Tell me what you saw.
openings.supervisor: You've stopped the job. Talk me through why.
openings.coworker: You waved me off — what's wrong?
openings.qa: You've held the work. What's the concern?
openings.hr: Tell me about a time you stopped a job. I want to hear how you'd say it.

turns.text: Understood. What do you need from me to make it safe?
The lads want to keep going. How do you tell them no?
Who else needs to know, right now?
Does any of the work already done need looking at again?

closing.text: You stopped it and you said why. That's exactly right — never apologise for that.

open.ask: You flagged something on line two. Tell me what you saw.

points.label: Say what you did about it

open.model: I stopped the job. There were sparks landing near the gas bottles in bay two with no screen up — that's a fire risk with oxy-fuel sitting right there. I've moved the lads back and held the work until we can screen it off.
open.why: Stop-work communication is judged on whether the person hearing it can act immediately. Fact, place, risk, what you already did — in that order.
open.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t0.ask: Understood. What do you need from me to make it safe?

points.label: Name the actual resource or action

t0.model: I need the bottles moved out of the bay and a screen between us and the walkway. Until that's done I'd rather we don't restart — I'll keep the area taped off.
t0.why: Stopping a job is only half the skill. Asking clearly for what would make it safe is what gets you taken seriously the second time.
t0.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t1.ask: The lads want to keep going. How do you tell them no?

points.label: Give the reason, not just the order
Point to the process or a person

t1.model: Look, I know we're behind, but we're not restarting until those bottles are moved — if a spark finds them nobody's going home. Safety's on their way now, five minutes.
t1.why: Saying no to your own workmates is the hardest English on a site. Firm, reason, respect, and point at the process rather than yourself.
t1.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t2.ask: Who else needs to know, right now?
t2.model: Supervisor and the safety officer straight away. Then whoever's working in the next bay, because the risk isn't only ours. And it wants writing up as a near miss.
t2.why: Escalation is a list, not one person: the boss, the people exposed, and the record.
t2.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t3.ask: Does any of the work already done need looking at again?

points.label: Show you thought about earlier work
Give a view with a reason
Defer to the inspector where appropriate

t3.model: The joints I ran this morning were before the extraction went down, so I think they're fine. Anything after about one o'clock I'd want the inspector to look at again before it goes out.
t3.why: Being able to reason about what your problem affects, and then hand the decision to the right person, is senior-level communication.
t3.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

codes.code: OSHA General Duty Clause, OSH Act Section 5(a)(1)
codes.title: Duty to provide a workplace free of recognised hazards

regulatory.requirement: Immediate halting of work when an imminent hazard is identified. Communication must be calm, direct and solutions-oriented.

benchmarks.must: Use assertive, professional, clear language to pause work without hostility or blame
Pinpoint the concrete threat explicitly — unshielded flammable vapours, inadequate local exhaust ventilation, and similar
State that work resumes only after an authorised inspector or safety officer clears the zone

simulations.title: Procedure Briefing
simulations.scenario: Explain a welding procedure and quality checks.

unexpectedEvents.message: One correction — the procedure was revised this morning. Have you got the new one?

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Procedure Briefing and make the sequence clearer.

openings.supervisor: New procedure on this job. Tell me back what you understand by it.
openings.qa: I'll be checking against the procedure. Tell me what it asks of you.
openings.coworker: We're both on this one. What did you take from the briefing?
openings.safety: The procedure's changed. What does that change for you on the floor?
openings.hr: Talk me through how you'd handle a procedure you've not used before.

turns.text: What would you do if the procedure and the drawing disagree?
If you're not certain about a step, what happens next?
How would you explain it to someone who missed the briefing?
Anything in it that changes how you protect yourself?

closing.text: Good. You repeated it back and you asked. That's how we avoid rework.

open.ask: New procedure on this job. Tell me back what you understand by it.

points.label: Repeat the instruction in your own words
Confirm or ask about anything unclear

open.model: So — pre-heat to a hundred, keep interpass under two-fifty, root with three-point-two and fill with four. Cap it in two runs, not one. Have I got that right?
open.why: Repeating an instruction back is the single most valuable habit in workplace English. It catches errors before they cost money and it proves you understood.
open.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t0.ask: What would you do if the procedure and the drawing disagree?

points.label: Say you do not choose between them
Say it should be recorded or clarified in writing

t0.model: I don't pick one — that's not my decision. I stop and take it to the supervisor and the welding engineer, and I'd want the answer in writing so the next man isn't guessing either.
t0.why: Conflicting documents are common on real projects. The correct answer is always: stop, escalate, get it in writing.
t0.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t1.ask: If you're not certain about a step, what happens next?

points.label: Say you do not start on a guess

t1.model: I ask before I start. Guessing on a procedure means the joint gets cut out, so two minutes with the supervisor is the cheap option.
t1.why: Every employer abroad worries that a welder with weaker English will nod rather than ask. Say explicitly that you ask.
t1.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t2.ask: How would you explain it to someone who missed the briefing?

points.label: Put it in plain, ordered steps

t2.model: Right — pre-heat to a hundred before you strike. Root with three-two, fill with four, and don't let it go over two-fifty between runs. Cap in two passes. Anything not clear?
t2.why: Teaching it back to someone else is the strongest proof that you understood, and supervisors abroad use it deliberately.
t2.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t3.ask: Anything in it that changes how you protect yourself?

points.label: Link the procedure to a hazard

t3.model: Pre-heated plate stays hot a long time, so heavier gloves and a warning to anyone else working near that bench. If we're going up in current there'll be more fume too, so extraction closer in.
t3.why: Connecting a procedure change to a safety consequence is exactly what a safety officer wants to hear from a welder.
t3.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

simulations.scenario: Check a drawing and request clarification before work.

unexpectedEvents.message: There's a revision B out on that drawing. You might be reading rev A.

openings.supervisor: You're holding on the drawing. What's not clear?
openings.coworker: I read it one way, you read it another. Tell me what you're seeing.
openings.safety: You've paused on the drawing. What's the issue?
openings.hr: Tell me how you handle a drawing you can't fully read.

turns.text: So what do you think it's asking for?
If I'm not available, who else would you ask?
Would you carry on and check later, or wait?
How would you record the answer so the next person has it?

closing.text: Asking cost you five minutes. Guessing would have cost us the panel.

open.ask: You had a question on the drawing. Which detail?

points.label: Say how you are reading it

open.model: Detail B, the joint at the base plate. The symbol reads as a six-mil fillet both sides to me, but the note underneath says full penetration. Which one governs?
open.why: A good drawing question is closed and answerable in one word. Point to the detail, say your reading, ask for a decision.
open.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t0.ask: So what do you think it's asking for?
t0.model: My reading is full penetration, because the note is specific and the symbol looks like it was carried over from the earlier revision. But I'd rather you confirm than I commit the joint.
t0.why: Employers want a welder who forms a view and still defers. Say what you think, why, and that you will accept correction.
t0.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t1.ask: If I'm not available, who else would you ask?

points.label: Name an alternative person or role
Say what you do while waiting

t1.model: The welding engineer, or the site supervisor if he's not about. I wouldn't guess — I'd move onto another joint that's clear and come back to this one.
t1.why: Knowing the second and third person to ask is what keeps work moving when the first one is busy.
t1.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t2.ask: Would you carry on and check later, or wait?

points.label: Show you understand production pressure too

t2.model: On something structural I wait — if it's wrong it gets cut out and that's a day gone. But I don't stand still, I move to a joint that is clear.
t2.why: The best answer shows you take quality seriously without pretending production does not matter.
t2.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t3.ask: How would you record the answer so the next person has it?
t3.model: I'd mark it on the drawing copy and note it in the log, and raise it as a query so it's on record. Then mention it at handover so the night shift isn't asking the same question.
t3.why: Recording a clarification once saves the same question being asked five times. It is a small habit that gets noticed.
t3.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

simulations.title: Construction Site Coordination
simulations.scenario: Coordinate welding work with another trade.

unexpectedEvents.message: Your hot work permit runs out in twenty minutes and there are scaffolders above you.

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Construction Site Coordination and make the handover clearer.

openings.supervisor: Site's busy today. Tell me what you need from the other trades to get your work done.
openings.coworker: Scaffolders are in your area. How do you want to work this?
openings.safety: There's hot work and other trades in the same zone. Talk me through it.
openings.qa: Your section's due for inspection. When will it be ready?
openings.hr: Describe how you work alongside other trades on a busy site.

turns.text: If someone's working below you, what do you say to them?
The electricians want the area for an hour. What do you tell them?
And if that pushes your work back — how do you let me know?
Give me a realistic time for inspection.

closing.text: That's the job on site. Half welding, half talking to people — you did both.

open.ask: Site's busy today. Tell me what you need from the other trades to get your work done.
open.model: I need the scaffold at the north face signed off before I can start, and the sparks out of that bay while I'm doing hot work. If they need an hour I can do the bench work first and go up after.
open.why: Site English is negotiation. What you need, from whom, by when, and what you can give — that last part is what gets you cooperation.
open.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t0.ask: If someone's working below you, what do you say to them?
t0.model: I'd go down and tell them face to face — I'm doing hot work above you, sparks and slag will come down. Either they move out for an hour or we get a blanket and a barrier under me.
t0.why: Shouting a warning is not communication if the person cannot act on it. Go to them, say the risk, offer the two options.
t0.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t1.ask: The electricians want the area for an hour. What do you tell them?

points.label: Attach a condition or a time

t1.model: They can have it, but I need it back by eleven or my inspection slips to tomorrow. I'll shut down and make it safe, and I'll let the supervisor know we've swapped.
t1.why: Agreeing with a condition and a time, then telling your own supervisor, is how site conflicts get avoided.
t1.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t2.ask: And if that pushes your work back — how do you let me know?
t2.model: I'd tell you now, not at the end of the shift. It's about two hours, which puts inspection into tomorrow morning. If that's a problem I could do the small joints tonight instead.
t2.why: Bad news early with an option attached is a senior habit. Bad news late with no option is what gets people replaced.
t2.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t3.ask: Give me a realistic time for inspection.
t3.model: Realistically tomorrow, first thing — I'd rather say that than promise tonight and have you turn up to joints that aren't cleaned. If the electricians are out by eleven I might get two ready today.
t3.why: Over-promising on time destroys trust faster than being slow. Commit, state the dependency, and be honest.
t3.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

regulatory.requirement: Multi-trade deconfliction to prevent fire, structural collapse, or exposure of nearby trades to arc radiation and toxic fumes.

benchmarks.must: Coordinate with nearby trades and set flash screens protecting them from UV arc rays
Verify a valid Hot Work Permit and establish a dedicated Fire Watch
Coordinate timing to avoid welding directly above or below another trade without overhead barrier protection

simulations.title: Quality Issue Report
simulations.scenario: Report an inspection concern and agree corrective action.

unexpectedEvents.message: Hold on. If that's on this batch, we shipped forty of them yesterday.

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Quality Issue Report and keep your language factual.

openings.qa: You've found something on the weld. Describe it to me.
openings.supervisor: You've come to me about a weld. What have you got?
openings.coworker: It's my weld you're looking at. Tell me straight — what's wrong?
openings.safety: A quality issue on a job. Does it affect anyone's safety?
openings.hr: Tell me about a time you had to report poor work. How did you put it?

turns.text: How did it get past? I'm not blaming anyone, I want to know.
Alright. What would you want me to do differently?
What do we do with the parts already finished?
And how do we stop it happening on the next batch?

closing.text: You described it clearly and you didn't hide it. That's the whole job.

open.ask: You've found something on the weld. Describe it to me.
open.model: There's undercut along the toe on the cap run, about forty mil long and it looks deeper than half a mil. That's outside what the spec allows, so I've held it rather than sending it through.
open.why: Defect reporting is precise language: name it, locate it, size it, then say why it matters. Vague reporting is why defects reach the customer.
open.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t0.ask: How did it get past? I'm not blaming anyone, I want to know.

points.label: Point at a cause, not a person
Take your share if it is yours

t0.model: Looking at it, the travel speed was too quick on that run and the access was awkward from that side. If it was mine I'll say so — I'd rather find the cause than argue about who.
t0.why: Answering a 'how did this happen' question without defending yourself is what makes an inspector trust you.
t0.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t1.ask: Alright. What would you want me to do differently?
t1.model: Maybe slow the cap run down and clean between passes — that's usually where the undercut creeps in. And if the access is that bad from the right, it might be worth turning the piece.
t1.why: Giving feedback to a colleague is the hardest professional English there is. Specific, reasoned, and collegial.
t1.source: General international workplace practice in fabrication, construction and oil and gas. Educational guidance only — requirements vary by employer, country and contract. Verify before you rely on it.

t2.ask: What do we do with the parts already finished?

points.label: Say they should be held or quarantined

t2.model: Anything from the same batch gets held until it's checked — we'd need to know which joints came off that setup. Nothing ships until the inspector's been over them.
t2.why: Containment thinking — 'what else might be affected' — is what quality systems are built on.
t2.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

t3.ask: And how do we stop it happening on the next batch?

points.label: Add a check or hold point
Say the team should be told

t3.model: Set a test piece at the start of each batch and have it looked at before we run the rest. And a two-minute toolbox talk so everyone knows what we found and why.
t3.why: Prevention answers separate a welder from a lead hand. Change, check, and tell the team.
t3.source: Framed on ISO 3834 quality-requirement thinking, widely used for industrial welding certification. Educational only — ISO 3834 certifies a company's quality system, not an individual welder.

unexpectedEvents.message: Permit's just been suspended — gas readings changed in the next bay.

openings.safety: This is a controlled area. Tell me what you need in place before you start.
openings.supervisor: Permit work today. Talk me through what you're waiting on.
openings.qa: Controlled work means everything is recorded. What are you signing for?
openings.coworker: I'm your fire watch. What do you need from me?
openings.hr: Describe how you prepare for work in a controlled or permit area.

turns.text: If the permit runs out mid-job, what do you do?
And what should I be watching for while you're working?
Who do you call if something changes in the area?
What has to be signed off before you leave?

closing.text: You waited, you checked, you asked. That's controlled work done properly.

open.ask: This is a controlled area. Tell me what you need in place before you start.

points.label: Mention atmosphere, isolation or gas checks
Mention a fire watch or standby

open.model: A hot work permit signed and in date, gas readings taken and still valid, the line isolated and locked, a fire watch with me, and an extinguisher and fire blanket at the bay. If any one of those is missing I don't start.
open.why: Controlled work has a checklist and employers expect you to recite it. Permit, tests, watch, emergency provision.
open.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t0.ask: If the permit runs out mid-job, what do you do?

points.label: Say you make the area safe first
Say the permit must be renewed or extended

t0.model: I stop. Make the area safe — gas off, everything cooled and clear — then go back to the permit issuer for an extension. You don't carry on under an expired permit, ever.
t0.why: This is a yes-or-no integrity question. Any hesitation reads badly. Stop, make safe, get it re-issued.
t0.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t1.ask: And what should I be watching for while you're working?

points.label: Give the watcher a specific job
Name what they should look for
Tell them what to do if it happens

t1.model: Watch behind and below me — that's where I can't see. Anything smoking or smouldering, or if you smell gas, tap me and I'll stop straight away. And please don't leave the bay until I'm cooled down and packed up.
t1.why: Briefing your own fire watch is a real workplace skill and most welders have never had to say it in English.
t1.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t2.ask: Who do you call if something changes in the area?
t2.model: Stop first, then the permit issuer and the safety officer. If it's gas or fire, the control room and get everyone out of the bay before anything else.
t2.why: Emergency escalation is about order: make it safe, warn people, then report.
t2.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

t3.ask: What has to be signed off before you leave?
t3.model: Permit closed out and handed back, fire watch held for the period after I finish, area cooled, leads and bottles cleared away, and a last walk round with you before I sign.
t3.why: Close-out is as regulated as start-up. Saying it shows you have actually worked in controlled areas.
t3.source: Established welding training practice — welding technology, standards and specifications, quality assurance and control, and destructive/non-destructive testing with work safety. Educational guidance only: confirm your employer's own procedure.

regulatory.requirement: Lockout/Tagout verification, atmospheric testing and safety barrier checks before entering a high-risk environment.

benchmarks.must: Verify completion and posting of a formal Confined Space or Hot Work entry permit

simulations.scenario: Present your experience and motivation to a hiring team.

unexpectedEvents.message: Sorry to cut in. Quick one from me — could you start Monday?

debrief.recommendedNextSimulation: Repeat Welding Interview and make your achievement example stronger.

openings.hr: Thanks for coming in. Start wherever you like — tell me about yourself.
openings.supervisor: I'll be your foreman if this goes well. Tell me what you can do.
openings.qa: I sit in on interviews for quality. Tell me about the standard of work you're used to.
openings.safety: I ask the safety questions. First though — tell me about your background.
openings.coworker: Informal one, this. I'm on the floor. What kind of welder are you?

turns.text: Give me an example of a difficult job you finished.
Tell me about a time you raised a safety concern.
How do you handle it when your work is rejected?
And why this company? What are you looking for next?

closing.text: That's everything from us. You explained your experience clearly — we'll be in touch.

open.ask: Thanks for coming in. Start wherever you like — tell me about yourself.

points.label: Say who you are and that you are a welder
Say how long you have been doing it
Name the processes you actually run
Say what you welded — product or sector
End with what you are looking for or ready to do

open.model: I'm a welder with six years' experience. I mostly run MIG and stick on structural steel — beams, columns and brackets for building frames. The last two years I was on a fabrication shop floor doing fit-up and welding, and I'm looking for work where I can move onto pipe.
open.why: The opening answer sets the whole interview. Four facts in twenty seconds, then stop and let them ask.
open.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t0.ask: Give me an example of a difficult job you finished.
t0.model: We had a tank repair with very tight access — you couldn't get square to the joint at all. I asked for a mirror and dropped the current so I could control the puddle from that angle, and I did a test piece first. It passed inspection first time and we finished the day early.
t0.why: This is the behavioural question every international employer asks. Situation, problem, what YOU did, result. Say 'I', not 'we', for the action part.
t0.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t1.ask: Tell me about a time you raised a safety concern.
t1.model: On a site in Douala I found a damaged welding lead with the copper showing. I stopped, tagged the set and took it to the supervisor rather than taping it up. They replaced the lead that morning and we started checking leads at the start of every shift.
t1.why: Employers abroad are legally exposed if you stay quiet. A concrete example with a real outcome is worth more than saying 'safety is my priority'.
t1.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t2.ask: How do you handle it when your work is rejected?
t2.model: It happens to everyone. I ask the inspector to show me exactly what failed and why, I put it right, and then I change whatever caused it. I'd rather it's caught in the shop than by the client.
t2.why: Interviewers use this to find out if you are defensive. Accept, ask why, fix, prevent — and never blame the inspector.
t2.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t3.ask: And why this company? What are you looking for next?

points.label: Say what you want to develop

t3.model: You do a lot of pipework and that's where I want to go — I've got the structural side solid and I want to get coded on pipe. I'm looking for somewhere I can stay and build up, not move every year.
t3.why: Vague answers here lose offers. Say something true about them, connect it to your experience, and name what you want to develop.
t3.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

openings.supervisor: You've come a long way. How would you describe yourself to a new employer?
openings.qa: If an inspector asked what standard you work to, what would you say?
openings.safety: How would you describe your approach to safety to someone who's never met you?

What part of your work do you still want to sharpen?
And what would you not compromise on?
Give me your closing line — the one you'd end an interview with.

closing.text: That's a professional answer. You're ready to go and have these conversations for real.

open.ask: Last conversation before you go out for roles. Tell me who you are professionally now.

points.label: Say what standard you work to

open.model: I'm a welder with six years behind me, mostly structural, MIG and stick, and I've spent the last year getting comfortable explaining my work in English. I work to the procedure and I stop when something isn't right. Next I want to get onto pipe and get coded.
open.why: This is your professional identity in four sentences — who, evidence, standard, direction. You will use it in every interview and every first day.
open.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t0.ask: What work are you aiming for next?

points.label: Name a specific type of work

t0.model: Pipe work, and eventually oil and gas. I know I won't walk straight into offshore, so the step I'm looking for is shop pipework where I can get the hours and get coded.
t0.why: Ambition with a realistic first step is credible. Ambition without one is not.
t0.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t1.ask: What part of your work do you still want to sharpen?

points.label: Say what you are doing about it

t1.model: Overhead and 6G — I can do them but I'm slow, and speed matters when you're being timed on a test. I'm practising on off-cuts and I want to sit a test on it this year.
t1.why: A real weakness with a plan attached builds trust. A fake weakness like 'I work too hard' destroys it instantly.
t1.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t2.ask: And what would you not compromise on?

points.label: Make it concrete, not a slogan

t2.model: Safety and not hiding a bad weld. If I'm behind and someone wants me to send a joint through that I know isn't right, I won't do it — I'll say so and take the argument.
t2.why: This is the answer that gets remembered. Make it concrete and admit it costs something.
t2.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.

t3.ask: Give me your closing line — the one you'd end an interview with.

points.label: Restate your value in one line

t3.model: Thank you for your time. I've got six years on structural, I turn up and I work to the procedure, and I'd like this job. Can I ask what the next step is?
t3.why: Most candidates end an interview by trailing off. Thanks, one line of value, say you want it, ask what happens next.
t3.source: Common structure for technical interviews with international contractors. Educational guidance only.
